2026-11-01|ls-rera-plots: RERA for plotted developments: what plot buyers must verify Land School · source: “RERA for Plotted Developments: What Plot Buyers Must Verify” by 1acre.in Key Highlights RERA is not an apartment law — plotted layouts fall inside it once they cross a size or amenity threshold. The commonly cited trigger: land above 500 sq m OR more than 8 plots (states vary slightly). A simple one-off land transfer between individuals, with no promised infrastructure, generally stays outside RERA. “RERA approved” is marketing language with no legal meaning — only registration on the state portal counts. Verification is minutes, free, and done by you — and can save years of dispute. What RERA for plotted development is The 2016 Act defines a “real estate project” broadly enough to cover developing land into plots for sale. Gated-plot communities, farm-plot schemes and ordinary layouts sit under the same registration, disclosure and escrow regime as towers. Four terms that get blurred: RERA registration (a verifiable number), “RERA approved” (a phrase with no defined status), NA permission (a separate land-use approval), and the Occupancy Certificate (local compliance — not a substitute for RERA’s protections). Untangling these is step one, because sellers use them interchangeably on purpose. What registration discloses The project’s portal page shows: the sanctioned layout (plots, roads, common areas); the land title behind it; the registration number that must match brochures and agreements exactly; the promised amenities the developer is now BOUND to deliver; the disclosed timeline; and the escrow confirmation that buyer money is ring-fenced for this project’s development. Definition — Escrow: a dedicated account where buyer payments must be spent on this project. It is what stops your road money funding somebody’s next launch. When registration becomes mandatory At the MARKETING stage — before the first sale agreement — once the layout crosses the threshold. And note the second trigger: promising shared infrastructure (roads, park, clubhouse, security) pulls a project into RERA REGARDLESS of size. The escrow protects instalments before delivery; registration also opens the authority’s complaint machinery to buyers after purchase. When a plotted sale is legitimately exempt A one-off land transfer between individuals with no promised development generally stays outside. Some states treat layouts where NA permission preceded the sale agreement as demarcated land sales. Agricultural land stays exempt while there is no active plan to convert and market it as a housing project. The rule for buyers: an exemption CLAIMED must be an exemption DOCUMENTED — ask what specifically justifies it, in writing. How to verify in minutes Check the triggers (size, plot count, promised amenities). Search the state portal by project name, promoter name or number. A genuine listing shows plans, approvals, title, timelines. Cross-check the number character-for-character against brochure and draft agreement — a mismatch, or no listing, is your answer. Red flags — and the checks that answer them Red flag What it usually means What to check Number does not match the portal Unregistered project — or someone else’s number Search the exact number on the official state portal yourself No mention of escrow Payments may not be ring-fenced Demand the escrow disclosure in the project details or agreement Exemption claimed, nothing shown Informal justification, not a legal one Request the NA permission or the exempting provision in writing “RERA approved” with no number Loose marketing, possibly zero compliance Ask for the number; verify independently Brochure amenities missing from the disclosure The promises may not be binding Compare brochure against the registered disclosure line by line RERA registered vs OC vs marketing claims Term What it actually confirms Where to verify RERA registered Formal registration, unique number, legal accountability State RERA portal “RERA approved” Nothing defined — a phrase No register exists; demand the number Occupancy Certificate Local safety/infrastructure compliance Municipal / planning authority RERA matters BEFORE you sign and pay; the OC matters near handover; the marketing phrase is always a claim to verify, never evidence. Example: The Amber Homes case near Hyderabad: an HMDA-approved layout never registered with RERA. A buyer paid over ₹1 crore for 1,000 sq yds, got half registered, and the regulator’s cease-and-desist arrived after the money. Approved layout, illegal selling — the two locks are different locks. Pre-purchase checklist ☐ Project found on the state portal by name or number. ☐ Number matches brochure and agreement exactly. ☐ Exemption claims backed by NA permission or the exempting clause, in writing. ☐ Promised amenities present in the registered disclosure. ☐ OC never treated as equivalent to RERA registration. ☐ Lawyer consulted when the status looks unclear. Quick answers (FAQ) Does RERA apply to all plot purchases? No — plain person-to-person land transfers without promised development are outside. Can a developer sell plots without registration? Not once the thresholds or amenity promises apply — that selling is illegal, with penalties. What if I buy into an unregistered project? You lose the escrow protection and the authority’s machinery; remedies shrink to ordinary contract suits. Bottom line Registration is not a formality a plot developer may skip. Once the threshold or an amenity promise is crossed, the number on the portal — not the phrase on the hoarding — is what protects a buyer. Verify it yourself, before signing, every time. For you: Your sequence as a developer is fixed: title → layout approval → RERA → marketing. And your fastest filter of other people’s ventures: “tell me the RERA number — I’ll look it up while we talk.” The reaction is the answer. 2026-11-01|ls-assigned-land: Assigned land: why it cannot be sold and what the law says Land School · source: “Assigned Land in India: Why It Cannot Be Sold and What the Law Says” by 1acre.in Key Highlights Assigned land = government surplus/wasteland granted to landless poor families for cultivation or house sites — possession and use, NOT free ownership. Transfers are prohibited or void under state land-reform laws; a registered sale deed changes nothing. The government can RESUME the land at any time, with no compensation to the buyer — and buying it can carry up to six months’ jail. Narrow exceptions: inheritance by heirs, bank mortgages, and good-faith pre-Act purchases by landless poor persons. The whole defence is two checks: the revenue record’s remarks and the Section 22-A prohibited list. What assigned land is Government surplus or wasteland handed to landless poor persons — typically agricultural labourers or SC/ST families — for cultivation or as a house site, under land-reform and welfare schemes. What transfers is possession and limited use rights; ownership stays CONDITIONAL with the state. The condition that matters to every buyer: the grant usually prohibits sale. Why the law bans its sale The point of assignment is welfare — land in the hands of the landless. If assignees could sell, the poor would be bought out for quick cash and the policy would defeat itself; so state laws (in Telangana, the Assigned Lands (Prohibition of Transfers) Act) bar selling, gifting, leasing or otherwise transferring without government permission, and declare violating transfers invalid. What “void ab initio” means Treated as if the transaction never legally happened — no title passes, ever. Even land that changed hands TEN times through ten registered deeds: every link is equally invalid. A registered document does not make you the owner here; the paper has no legal weight at all. One narrow protection exists: a landless poor person who bought in good faith, for value, from the original assignee BEFORE the Act commenced and was in possession on that date — it protects the poor, not an investor. Definition — Void ab initio: void “from the beginning” — not cancelled later, but never valid at any moment. Nothing downstream of it can be valid either. What happens if it is sold anyway The government can resume the land at ANY time — no limitation period runs in its favour going away — and reassign it to another eligible landless family. The buyer gets no compensation; no civil court can decree the sale into existence. And the consequence sellers never mention: acquiring assigned land in breach of the prohibition is an OFFENCE carrying up to six months’ imprisonment. The buyer is not just a victim in this law’s eyes. Transferability by land category Category Freely transferable? Notes Patta (private) land Yes Ordinary sale deed + registration Assigned land No Transfer void; resumption + penal risk Tribal-area land Highly restricted Transfers to non-tribals barred in scheduled areas Ceiling-surplus land No Vested in government for redistribution Endowment (temple) land No Alienation needs statutory sanction, rarely given Forest land No Central law bars de-reservation without approval What an assignee CAN do Cultivate for the family; pass the land to legal heirs (inheritance is generally not a prohibited transfer); mortgage it to a scheduled bank, co-operative or notified institution — the one security the Act permits; build a house where the assignment was a house site. And in some states, apply to the Collector for DE-RESTRICTION — converting it into regular patta land eligible for sale once eligibility conditions are met. Rules vary; the revenue authority’s word is the only one that counts. How to check whether a plot is assigned Pull the latest Record of Rights from the state revenue department and read the REMARKS column for “assigned”, “granted” or restriction notes. Check the state’s prohibited-property register (Section 22-A list) for the survey number. Ask the local revenue office directly. And read the original ASSIGNMENT ORDER — it states plainly whether transfer is prohibited. Fifteen minutes of record-reading is the difference between owning land and owning a legal dead end. Example: The classic Hyderabad-belt trap: a corridor plot at 40% below market, seller waving a registered deed from a 2009 purchase. The RoR remarks column reads “asgd”. That deed — and the one before it — are both void; the discount was the disclosure. Walk away; no lawyer can cure it. If you are the assignee wanting to sell Apply to the competent revenue authority for removal of the transfer restriction where state law permits, BEFORE entering any agreement. For SC/ST or tribal-origin land, confirm whether Collector approval is mandatory. Selling first and regularising later is not a sequence the law recognises. Quick answers (FAQ) Can assigned land be sold after N years? No automatic ripening — only formal de-restriction changes its status. Why do registered deeds exist on assigned land? Because registration only blocks parcels actually on the prohibited list; the registrar’s stamp never validates a void transfer. Can family inherit it? Yes — heirs succeed; that is not a prohibited transfer. Can it be mortgaged? Only to banks/institutions the Act permits. Can it ever become freehold? In some states, via Collector-approved conversion to patta land. Bottom line Assigned land is the one category where late homework has NO remedy — no cure, no compensation, no sympathetic court. The RoR remarks and the 22-A list, checked before any money moves, are the entire safeguard. For you: For a plotting developer this is the first gate on every parcel — before price, before layout dreams: Dharani/RoR remarks + 22-A check on each survey number. One assigned survey number inside an assembled venture can poison the whole layout’s marketability. Make the check a fixed line item in your acquisition template. Glossary — every term, simply SIR (Special Intensive Revision) A nationwide exercise by the Election Commission to re-check and rebuild electoral rolls from scratch, intended to remove duplicate, dead or ineligible voters. Example: it is similar in spirit to a housing society re-verifying every resident’s name against ID proof before printing a new register — necessary in principle, but capable of wrongly dropping a real resident if the verification is rushed or poorly targeted. CEC (Chief Election Commissioner) The head of the three-member Election Commission of India, appointed by the President on the government’s recommendation (under a process set by a 2023 law), and removable only through a judicial-impeachment-style process. Example: comparable in insulation from everyday political pressure to a Supreme Court judge, at least on paper. Electoral roll The official list of everyone registered to vote in a given constituency; being removed from it means being unable to vote there even if otherwise eligible. Example: like being removed from a building’s resident register — you can still live there, but you can’t vote in the society’s elections until you’re re-added. ‘Vote chori’ (vote theft) A political slogan, not a legal term, used by the opposition INDIA bloc to describe what it alleges is systematic, deliberate removal of genuine voters (rather than honest clean-up of duplicate or dead entries) that benefits the ruling party. Example: the term functions like “scam” in Indian political shorthand — a label applied before, not after, any formal finding. Vanara sena / Ravana (Ramayana reference) In the Hindu epic Ramayana, Lord Rama’s army of monkey-warriors (the “vanara sena”), led by Hanuman, helps him defeat the ten-headed demon king Ravana and rescue his wife Sita. Example: Indian politicians very commonly borrow this story's good-versus-evil structure to cast their own side as Rama’s army and a rival as Ravana — it is rhetorical costume, not a claim about facts. INDIA bloc Short for the opposition alliance formed in 2023 to jointly contest the ruling BJP-led NDA (National Democratic Alliance); includes Congress and multiple regional parties that otherwise often compete against each other in their own states. Example: like rival cricket franchises temporarily fielding a combined XI against one shared opponent. Ramlila Maidan A large public ground in central Delhi historically used for staging the biggest political rallies in Indian politics, including some that have helped topple national governments. Example: its symbolic weight is similar to a political party choosing to hold its biggest rally at a city’s most historically significant public square rather than any ordinary stadium. TPCC (Telangana Pradesh Congress Committee) The Congress party's formal state-level organisational unit for Telangana, headed in this story by B. Mahesh Kumar Goud. Example: functions like a state branch office of a national company, with its own local head answerable to the national headquarters. South Central Railway (SCR) / Railway zone Indian Railways is divided into zones for operational management; SCR covers Telangana and parts of neighbouring states and answers to the central Railway Board, not any state government. Example: like a regional branch of a nationally-owned utility company — locally present, but centrally controlled. Article 324 of the Constitution The constitutional provision establishing the Election Commission of India and setting out the (judicial-impeachment-style) process for removing a Chief Election Commissioner. Example: the same basic design logic as the protection given to Supreme Court judges — meant to keep the officer insulated from ordinary political pressure. 4. The backstory — how we got here Date Event Through 2026 The Election Commission runs the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls nationally; opposition parties say roughly 13–13.5 crore names are deleted in the process, a figure this edition could not independently verify. Tue, 27 Oct 2026 South Central Railway declines Telangana Congress’s request for five special trains to carry roughly 15,000 workers to the planned 1 November Delhi rally. Wed, 28 Oct 2026 Telangana Congress workers protest outside SCR headquarters in Secunderabad; police detain some protesters. The party pivots to arranging roughly 150–200 private buses instead. Sun, 1 Nov 2026 The INDIA bloc’s “Vote Bachao, Desh Bachao” rally is held at Ramlila Maidan, Delhi. Rahul Gandhi, Kharge, Mamata Banerjee, Akhilesh Yadav and Revanth Reddy all speak; Revanth Reddy makes the “vanara sena”/“Ravana” remark; BJP calls it “disgraceful” and disputes turnout. The deeper forces at work here run well beyond one rally. Disputes over the accuracy and fairness of India’s electoral rolls are not new — similar flashpoints have recurred around National Register of Citizens debates in Assam and West Bengal, and around state-specific roll revisions in Bihar earlier in the SIR cycle. What is specific to this moment is the scale of the claimed deletions (13-plus crore names, if the opposition’s figure holds up) landing in the run-up to a dense multi-state election calendar, which raises the stakes of any roll dispute far above a routine administrative housekeeping exercise. A ten-year follower of Indian politics would also recognise the Ramayana-framing device itself as a well-worn tool — Indian politicians across the spectrum have cast rivals as various mythological villains for decades — and would read Revanth Reddy’s remark less as news in itself and more as a data point on how combative Telangana’s Congress leadership is willing to be on the national stage, which is the more durable signal for Vivek to track. 5. So what — stakes and consequences The rally and the remark both serve fairly narrow, short-term purposes for each side. Revanth Reddy and Telangana Congress gain visibility and base-energising theatre at minimal real cost — a sharp quote costs nothing administratively. The BJP gains a clean, quotable “disgraceful” counter-line and a turnout dispute that lets it avoid engaging with the underlying SIR deletion numbers directly. The Election Commission, notably, said nothing in any source found in this edition’s research — it is the subject of the rally, not a participant in the day’s exchange of quotes. Watch: (a) whether the Election Commission or CEC Gyanesh Kumar's office issues any formal response to the resignation demand (moderate likelihood of a terse statement, low likelihood of any actual resignation); (b) whether SIR-related deletion disputes surface specifically in Telangana or Hyderabad in the coming weeks, given a separate (pre-window) report of steep Hyderabad voter-roll cuts under SIR; (c) whether the Miyapur land-auction Cabinet decision slips further while the Chief Minister’s public bandwidth stays focused on national rallies (plausible, unconfirmed); (d) whether the Railways-Congress train dispute recurs ahead of any future Delhi mobilisation. What this means for you: (a) For Hyderabad/Telangana real estate specifically: nothing here changes any title, approval or auction directly, but a Chief Minister and ruling party visibly consumed by national political combat is a soft signal that administratively heavy decisions sitting with his Cabinet — the Miyapur auction foremost among them — may move slower than the political announcements around them suggest. Price that lag into any plan that assumes a near-term Miyapur auction. (b) For business and investment generally: voter-roll disputes at this scale are a leading indicator of how contested the next election cycle will be, which tends to correlate with how much a ruling party leans on populist land/resource announcements (free land for the poor, auction proceeds to welfare schemes) rather than steady administrative process in the run-up to polls. The beginner’s mistake is to read this story as pure noise with zero relevance to a plotting developer's business and skip it entirely. The sharper, expert read is narrower but real: this is a bandwidth and tempo signal, not a land-policy signal — it tells you how to pace your own expectations of government decision-making speed this month, not what any decision will be. 6. The 20% that gives you 100% — your keep-forever map Telangana's Congress Chief Minister used a mythological insult against the Prime Minister at a huge opposition rally in Delhi, protesting a national voter-roll exercise his own party says has wrongly deleted over 13 crore names; his own party's workers got there by bus after the Railways refused them special trains, which both sides read through their own political lens. None of it changes a single land record, approval or rupee in Telangana today. What it changes is where the state's top political attention is currently pointed — toward Delhi and national electoral combat, not toward the Cabinet decisions on land sitting in Hyderabad. When a state's top leadership is visibly absorbed in national political theatre, expect pending administrative decisions in that state to slow, not accelerate. Numbers cited by any one political side (here, the 13–13.5 crore deletion figure) are claims to be tracked, not facts to be repeated as settled. A dispute between a state party unit and a central-government-controlled body (here, Congress vs. the Railways) is a reliable, recurring template for Centre-State friction stories — recognise the shape, not just this instance. Rhetorical escalation (a jail threat against a constitutional officer, a personal dare back) is a sign both sides believe the underlying issue has genuine public traction — worth tracking the substance even when the specific quotes are theatre. 2026-11-02|ls-capital-gains: Capital gains tax on agricultural land sale Land School · source: “Capital Gains Tax on Agricultural Land Sale in India” by 1acre.in Key Highlights Rural agricultural land is NOT a capital asset under Section 2(14)(iii) — its sale attracts no capital gains tax at all. The rural test is mechanical: the nearest municipality’s census population, and aerial distance of 2 / 6 / 8 km. Urban agricultural land is taxed like any property; long-term starts at 24 months. Section 54B exemption needs TWO years of actual farming before sale, reinvestment in farmland within two years, and a three-year lock-in on the new land. Section 50C lets the taxman substitute the stamp-duty value when you sell below it. When the tax applies at all One question decides everything: is the land RURAL or URBAN under the Income Tax Act? Rural agricultural land is excluded from the very definition of a capital asset by Section 2(14)(iii) — no capital asset, no capital gain, nothing to tax. Urban agricultural land gets no carve-out and is taxed like any other asset. Two owners can sell what looks like the same plot and one pays nothing while the other owes tax on the whole gain — purely because of where the land sits. The rural test — mechanical, not agricultural Nothing to do with how the land is farmed; everything to do with location and population. Land is RURAL if it lies outside a municipality or cantonment of 10,000+ people, AND outside these aerial distances from those limits: 2 km where the population is 10,000–1 lakh; 6 km where it is 1–10 lakh; 8 km where it exceeds 10 lakh. Population comes from the last published census; distance is measured AERIALLY — as the crow flies, not as the road winds. Inside the limits = urban agricultural land = taxable. One nuance: the exemption attaches to the LAND — a farmhouse, well or standing trees sold in the same deal are valued and treated separately. Example: Two farmers sell near Hyderabad (population >10 lakh, so the 8 km band applies). One’s land sits 9 km aerially from the municipal limit — rural, gain fully exempt. The other’s sits 7 km out — urban, fully taxable. Same crop, same buyer profile, two kilometres of geometry worth lakhs in tax. The second test: was it actually farmed? Classification decides the tax; CULTIVATION decides whether your claim survives scrutiny. Revenue records carry seasonal cultivation entries — the evidence that agricultural operations actually happened — and Section 54B leans on exactly that record for its two-year farming condition. Land held bare as pure investment is where exemption claims die at assessment. How the gain is computed Sale price minus purchase cost and expenses. Held 24+ months: long-term. The current long-term regime taxes gains at 12.5% without indexation (indexation having been withdrawn for post-July-2024 sales). And Section 50C looms over the price itself: sell below the stamp-duty value and the department can treat THAT value as your deemed sale price, subject to a tolerance margin — the guideline value quietly setting your tax floor. Rural vs urban at a glance Aspect Rural agricultural land Urban agricultural land Capital asset? No — s.2(14)(iii) excludes it Yes Capital gains tax None LTCG/STCG as applicable TDS on sale (194-IA) Expressly excluded 1% at ₹50 lakh+ (resident seller) Exemption routes Not needed 54B (farmland), 54EC (bonds) The exits: 54B and 54EC Section 54B — individuals and HUFs: reinvest the gain in NEW agricultural land within two years, provided the sold land was farmed for the two years before sale; money not yet reinvested by the return-filing date parks in a Capital Gains Account Scheme; the new land locks in for three years — sell early and the exemption unwinds. Section 54EC — the alternative for long-term gains: NHAI/REC/PFC/IRFC bonds within six months (₹50 lakh cap, five-year lock). The taxes that ride alongside TDS: buyers deduct 1% under 194-IA on urban agricultural land at ₹50 lakh+ — rural land is expressly outside the section. NRI sellers: Section 195 instead, at much higher rates — plan with a lower-deduction certificate. 50C: as above, the stamp-value floor. Quick answers (FAQ) Is rural agricultural land exempt? Fully — it is not a capital asset. How is “rural” defined? The census-population + aerial-distance test above. Indexation still available? Not under the current 12.5% regime. Urban land exemptions? 54B with the farming and lock-in conditions; 54EC bonds. TDS on farmland? Urban yes (₹50L+), rural no. Don’t want to buy farmland again? 54EC bonds, or pay the 12.5% and stay liquid. Bottom line Before selling any farmland, establish three things in writing: the aerial distance to the nearest 10,000+ municipality, the census figure that sets the band, and the cultivation record. Those three lines decide whether the tax is zero, exempt-with-conditions, or fully payable — get a CA’s letter where kilometres decide lakhs. For you: For your JD landowner partners this is THE conversation: many Ranga Reddy parcels sit inside Hyderabad’s 8 km band — urban, taxable — while one village further out is exempt. Knowing which side of the line a family’s land falls (and flagging 54B’s two-year farming condition early) makes you the developer who saved them lakhs before the deal even signed. 2026-11-02|ls-mutation: Mutation of land records: what it is and why it matters Land School · source: “Mutation of Land Records: What It Is and Why It Matters” by 1acre.in Key Highlights Mutation updates the owner’s name in the government’s revenue register after sale, inheritance, gift or partition — it does NOT transfer ownership; registration did that. Skipping it is a top reason buyers fight tax notices and loan rejections years after a purchase. The name changes by state — dakhil kharij, intiqal, patta transfer, khata transfer — the process is the same. A DISPUTED claim cannot be mutated by a revenue officer: it goes to civil court first. The Supreme Court’s position cuts both ways: mutation is not proof of title — but its ABSENCE is proof something was never finished. What mutation is The update of the government’s revenue register to show the CURRENT owner’s name after a sale, inheritance, gift or partition. It is different from the sale deed and registration: mutation affects the tax and revenue record and does not by itself prove legal title. Rural land mutates at the revenue office; urban property at the municipal corporation. The application typically needs the sale deed, previous mutation records and identity proof — and it matters for paying property tax under the right name, and for every future loan or resale. Definition — Mutation (dakhil kharij / khata transfer / patta transfer): the state updating its own ledger of who holds the land — the bridge between the registered deed and the revenue record. Registration changes OWNERSHIP; mutation changes the government’s BOOKS. What the process verifies Not a rubber stamp. The reviewing officer checks that the applicant is the rightful new owner based on a valid transfer document — sale deed, gift deed, or inheritance record — and cross-checks the property’s survey number, area and boundaries against the existing revenue record. What the exercise CANNOT do: establish or guarantee title. It aligns the ledger; it does not adjudicate ownership — which is why a disputed claim goes to civil court, not the Tehsildar. Documents by route How the land came to you Core document for mutation Purchase Registered sale deed Gift Registered gift deed Inheritance (no will) Death certificate + legal-heir certificate Inheritance (will) Death certificate + will (probate where applicable) Partition Registered partition deed / decree Most state portals also want the latest tax receipt and identity proof, whatever the route. One heir applying while others exist? Expect to produce their no-objection letters and an indemnity bond. Why it matters An unmutated register keeps showing the OLD owner though the sale is legally complete. Consequences compound: tax bills keep going to the previous owner while unpaid dues attach to the LAND, not the person; banks reject loans because mutation status is a basic ownership check; resale gets harder because the next buyer’s advocate flags the mismatch instantly; and heir disputes drag for years while land sits under a deceased owner’s name. Example: A buyer purchases in 2018, never mutates. In 2024 a tax-arrears notice arrives — the previous owner’s unpaid dues, now attached to the land. Then the bank declines a mortgage: “record shows a different owner”. Two problems, one skipped application that would have taken a few weeks in 2018. When to apply Immediately after any transaction — some states now run online or even automated mutation for straightforward transfers, others still take manual applications at the revenue office. The two classic delays: assuming the sale deed alone is enough, and inherited land sitting unmutated across a generation. Buying land that moved informally within a family? Ask whether mutation was completed at EACH step, not just the latest. Buying? Check mutation status first The seller-vs-record match is precisely the check that fails on an unmutated parcel — and it is checkable from outside (Dharani in Telangana shows the current pattadar). A mismatch does not always mean fraud; it always means an unfinished step someone must complete before your money moves. Quick answers (FAQ) Does mutation transfer ownership? No — registration does; mutation records it. How long does it take? Weeks for clean files; longer with objections. Can I sell unmutated land? Legally the registered owner can — practically, buyers and their banks balk; mutate first. Heir dispute during mutation? The revenue officer steps aside; civil court decides. Need a lawyer? Not for a clean application; yes the moment there is an objection. Mandatory for agricultural land? Effectively yes — the revenue record drives everything from tax to crop entries. Does it affect loans? Directly — lenders treat it as a gating check. Bottom line Easy to postpone, expensive to ignore. Mutation keeps your name accurate in the records that decide your tax bill, your loan eligibility and your next sale — apply promptly, and when buying, treat the seller’s mutation status as part of the title check. For you: Build it into your buyer experience: hand every plot purchaser a mutation-application pack at registration (or file it for them). Ventures whose buyers’ records are clean resell faster — and resales are your best advertising. On the acquisition side: an unmutated seller is a seller who cannot close on your timeline; surface it in week one, not at the SRO. Plain English: this is recycled water, not drinking water, aimed specifically at the large-volume uses that never needed drinking-quality water in the first place. Mechanics: the water is drawn from STPs across the city rather than from reservoirs, so every litre used this way is a litre that does not have to come from Singur or Manjira. Chief Minister Revanth Reddy directed that treated-water use become mandatory for specified non-potable purposes within Greater Hyderabad’s civic bodies, with the Secretariat and Chief Minister’s Office landscaping named as an explicit test case. Plain English: the clearest, hardest obligation reported so far falls on government premises, not private builders. Incentives: large, visible IT-park landlords make useful early adopters for officials — compliance by a handful of big, reputation-conscious names generates press coverage and social proof without the government having to write and enforce a blanket rule for thousands of smaller builders at once. Who’s who and what’s what — the dossiers HMWSSB (Hyderabad Metropolitan Water Supply & Sewerage Board) What it is: the statutory utility responsible for drinking-water supply and sewerage/STPs across Greater Hyderabad, created by the Hyderabad Metropolitan Water Supply and Sewerage Act, 1989. Backstory: formed by the then-undivided Andhra Pradesh government on 1 November 1989, which is why today’s launch fell on its 37th Foundation Day. Power map: answers to the state’s Municipal Administration & Urban Development (MA&UD) department, which the Chief Minister currently holds personally; its Managing Director reports up that chain, and HYDRAA, GHMC and HMDA are peer agencies it coordinates with rather than controls. Backstory: leads the Congress government that won the 2023 Telangana Assembly election, ending a decade of BRS rule; retains the Municipal Administration & Urban Development portfolio for himself rather than assigning it to a separate minister, alongside General Administration, Law & Order and all unallocated departments. Why he’s in this story: because he personally holds the MA&UD portfolio, a water-utility operational launch like this one runs through his own office rather than a separate minister’s — he directed the mandatory-use order and personally congratulated HMWSSB staff on Foundation Day. Power map: answers to the Telangana Legislative Assembly and the Congress central leadership; BRS (KTR, Harish Rao) and BJP (state unit, Amit Shah) are his principal rivals. Bias note: the outlets reporting his congratulatory remarks (Siasat, The Print, local Telugu press) are generally sympathetic or neutral wire-style reports of a government press release, not independent investigative pieces. K. Ashok Reddy What it is: Managing Director, HMWSSB, as of the most recent (February 2026) confirmation found. Why he’s in this story: as MD, he was the official quoted in this paper’s 17 October coverage on quality norms and enforcement for the scheme, and remains the senior operational officer accountable for whether today’s launch actually works. Power map: reports to the MA&UD department (effectively the Chief Minister’s office); oversees HMWSSB’s Joint Managing Director and Executive Directors. Mayank Mittal, IAS What it is: HMWSSB’s Joint Managing Director, a post created in the board’s 2026 restructuring (he was previously an Executive Director at the board). Why he’s in this story: represents the expanded leadership structure HMWSSB built in 2026 alongside the three-way split of GHMC into separate municipal corporations — relevant backdrop to why the board has been reorganising its capacity just as it launches a new operational scheme. CREDAI, NAREDCO & the Telangana Builders Federation What they are: the three principal developer/builder industry associations operating in Hyderabad — CREDAI and NAREDCO are national bodies with active Telangana chapters; the Telangana Builders Federation is a state-level body. Why they’re in this story: they are the bodies that “assured cooperation” at HMWSSB’s mid-October meeting, before the scheme’s tariff or volume target were settled — effectively the collective voice of Vivek’s own peer group in these negotiations. Incentive: public cooperation protects member builders from being singled out individually as water rationing tightens, and buys them a seat at the table while scheme rules are still being written. Mindspace Business Parks What it is: a large Hyderabad-based commercial real estate operator running IT/business-park campuses (publicly listed as a REIT), promoted by the K Raheja Corp group. Why it’s in this story: named by NewsMeter as one of the private campuses specifically asked by officials to switch construction, gardening and landscaping water to the treated supply — one of the scheme’s first visible private test cases. Raheja Group (K Raheja Corp) What it is: a major Mumbai-headquartered real estate and retail group with a large Hyderabad commercial portfolio, the promoter behind Mindspace. Why it’s in this story: named alongside Mindspace as a private landlord asked to adopt treated water for non-potable uses on its properties. HYDRAA (Hyderabad Disaster Response and Asset Protection Agency) What it is: a Telangana state agency created under the current Congress government, originally focused on reclaiming lake Full Tank Level (FTL) and buffer-zone land from encroachment through demolitions. Backstory: has faced repeated Telangana High Court criticism over the adequacy of its proof before ordering demolitions. Why it’s in this story: reported as the agency tasked with inspecting construction sites for water-use compliance under this scheme — a new, non-demolition role being added to an agency the public mostly associates with bulldozers. Power map: answers to the state government; distinct from, but coordinates with, HMWSSB, GHMC and HMDA. NGT (National Green Tribunal) What it is: India’s specialised environmental court, with statutory authority over pollution-control and environmental-clearance disputes. Why it’s in this story: sets the water-quality standards that treated wastewater must meet before reuse under this scheme; has also separately pushed Hyderabad for years over untreated sewage flowing into the Musi river and Hussain Sagar lake, part of the broader regulatory pressure behind the city’s STP expansion. Singur & Manjira reservoirs What they are: two of the upstream reservoirs that supply a share of Hyderabad’s piped drinking water. Why they’re in this story: this paper’s 17 October coverage reported both under pressure from an El Niño-linked rainfall deficit, cited by HMWSSB’s MD as the direct reason for pushing construction and other bulk non-drinking users onto treated water instead — the entire scheme exists to protect these reservoirs’ drinking-water supply. Chief Secretary Sanjay Jaju What it is: Telangana’s senior-most civil servant. Why he’s in this story: announced, on 13 October, an additional 20 MGD draw from the Mallannasagar project from November — a parallel, administrative-level drought response that sits in the same policy window as this scheme, made by a civil servant rather than an elected minister, which this paper’s earlier coverage read as a sign of this government managing an unpopular topic (water rationing) through technical channels rather than headline politics. 3. Glossary — every term, simply HMWSSB — Hyderabad Metropolitan Water Supply & Sewerage Board, the city’s water utility. Think of it as the single company that both pipes drinking water into your home and pipes sewage away from it. STP (Sewage Treatment Plant) — a facility that cleans used/waste water (sewage) to a standard safe for reuse in specific non-drinking applications, or safe to release into a river or lake. Hyderabad has dozens of STPs along the Musi river and elsewhere, with total installed capacity reported in the thousand-plus MLD range. MLD / MGD — Million Litres per Day and Million Gallons per Day, the two units Indian water utilities use for large volumes; one MGD is roughly 4.55 MLD. Reports on this scheme mix both units, which is part of why figures sometimes look inconsistent across outlets. Non-potable water — water that is not safe or certified for drinking, but is perfectly fine for uses like curing concrete, dust suppression, watering gardens or flushing — the entire category this scheme targets. Treated wastewater reuse — taking sewage that has already been cleaned at an STP and using it again for a non-drinking purpose, instead of releasing it into a river/lake or letting it go to waste. A simple example: instead of pumping fresh borewell water onto a construction site to settle dust, a tanker brings STP-treated water instead. El Niño — a recurring Pacific Ocean warming pattern that, in India, is often associated with weaker monsoon rainfall. This year’s El Niño-linked rainfall deficit is the stated trigger for Telangana’s whole drought-response programme, this scheme included. NGT (National Green Tribunal) — a specialised Indian court that only hears environmental cases, with the power to set binding standards (like treated-water reuse quality) and order clean-up or compensation. Green Water Tanker / ‘Dial-a-Green Tanker’ — the branded name for this scheme’s delivery fleet; tankers carrying treated wastewater, distinguished from HMWSSB’s ordinary drinking-water tankers by special branding and (reportedly) GPS tracking. Command Control Centre — HMWSSB’s central monitoring room, intended to track tanker bookings, GPS locations and deliveries for this scheme in real time, the way a cab-aggregator tracks its fleet. Tariff — the price per unit of water a bulk user (like a builder) would pay; for this scheme, still unpublished as of today’s search, which is the single biggest open question for anyone trying to budget against it. Bulk user — a water-utility term for a large-volume consumer (a builder, factory or big housing complex) as opposed to an individual household, usually billed on a different tariff structure. CREDAI / NAREDCO — Confederation of Real Estate Developers’ Associations of India / National Real Estate Development Council, the two largest national industry bodies representing property developers, both with active Telangana chapters. Foundation Day — the anniversary of an institution’s founding; HMWSSB chose its own 37th Foundation Day (1 November) as the ceremonial launch date for this scheme, a common Indian government practice of pairing a policy announcement with an institutional milestone for publicity value. HYDRAA — Hyderabad Disaster Response and Asset Protection Agency, a Telangana state agency best known for demolishing structures encroaching on lake buffer zones, now also reportedly inspecting construction-site water compliance. 4. The backstory — how we got here Date What happened 1 Nov 1989 HMWSSB established under the Hyderabad Metropolitan Water Supply and Sewerage Act, 1989. 2023 Reported STP capacity around 714 MLD across roughly 20 plants, with more under construction. 18 Sept 2026 Telangana Assembly resolution seeks a ₹20,000-crore Central drought relief package for drought-hit mandals. 24 Sept 2026 HMWSSB asks private STP owners citywide to register as certified treated-water suppliers, subject to quality inspection. 12 Oct 2026 CM Revanth Reddy chairs a special El Niño review, calls the drought “a disaster comparable to the Covid-19 pandemic.” 13 Oct 2026 Chief Secretary Sanjay Jaju announces an extra 20 MGD draw from Mallannasagar from November. 16 Oct 2026 HMWSSB meets CREDAI, NAREDCO and the Telangana Builders Federation; announces 1 November launch, no tariff/volume/booking details yet (this paper’s 17 Oct Deep Dive). 31 Oct 2026 Tanker booking process reportedly due to open, a day ahead of launch. 1 Nov 2026 (Sun) Scheme launches at the Secretariat on HMWSSB’s 37th Foundation Day; CM orders mandatory treated-water use for civic bodies; Mindspace and Raheja asked to switch. 2–3 Nov 2026 Wider press coverage of the launch, naming the private test cases and HYDRAA’s inspection role — today’s window. The deeper force behind all of this is simple hydrology meeting city growth: Hyderabad’s drinking-water reservoirs (Singur, Manjira, and the Krishna/Godavari-linked schemes) were sized for an earlier, smaller city, and a construction boom plus a weak monsoon year puts the two main demand sources — households and building sites — into direct competition for the same shrinking supply. The water board’s structural answer, visible across 2025–26, has been to build a second, parallel supply chain out of a resource the city used to simply discard: its own sewage. What a ten-year follower of Hyderabad’s water politics knows that a first-time reader does not: HMWSSB has announced treated-water reuse initiatives before without durable follow-through — a 2014-era commercial reuse tariff that never became a city-wide norm is the clearest precedent, and it is the only tariff figure available even today. The pattern this paper’s own coverage has now tracked twice (17 October and today) is that HMWSSB is reliably good at hitting an announced launch date and reliably slow at publishing the commercial terms — tariff, volume targets, enforcement — that turn a launch into a functioning market. 5. So what — stakes and consequences Who wins: HMWSSB gains a new, non-reservoir revenue stream and some relief on Singur/Manjira draw; gated communities with their own STPs gain a buyer for water they used to simply discharge; the city gains a small reduction in drinking-water demand at a moment of real stress. Who is exposed: any builder who has not yet planned for a possible switch, or who assumes the current drinking-water tanker/borewell arrangement will remain unquestioned as HYDRAA’s inspection role expands; and, less visibly, builders smaller than Mindspace or Raheja, who are not yet named individually but who may be next once the scheme’s mechanics (tariff, app, enforcement) actually mature. Watch: a published tariff order in the coming weeks (likely, given the booking app and GPS-tankers are already built — the commercial layer is usually the last piece); HYDRAA inspections at private construction sites beyond Mindspace/Raheja within one to two months (possible, but this paper’s own tracking of similar announcements suggests enforcement tends to lag); and a clarification on whether use is legally mandatory or simply encouraged for private builders (probable within this quarter, since the ambiguity itself is becoming a story). What this means for you: (a) for Hyderabad/Telangana real estate — treat this as the early phase of a real shift in how construction sites will have to source water in a stressed city; a plotting developer running active sites should start asking HMWSSB’s zonal office now whether treated-water booking is actually available in their layout’s area, rather than waiting for a tariff notification that may take months; (b) for business/investment generally — this is a textbook case of a government converting an environmental constraint (drought) into a new regulated market (treated-water sales) rather than just a blanket restriction, which tends to create a genuine commercial opportunity for whoever moves early (tanker operators, STP equipment vendors, water-quality testing firms) once the rules firm up. Beginner mistake: reading “scheme launches” and assuming it is now mandatory, priced and bookable everywhere in the city. Sharper expert read: a launch date being met while the tariff, final volume target and legal mandate for private builders all remain unpublished is itself the story — the real signal is how long that gap stays open, not the flag-off ceremony. 6. The 20% that gives you 100% — your keep-forever map Facing a rainfall-deficit year, Hyderabad’s water utility spent six weeks turning an October promise into a real, if still unpriced, fleet of tankers that deliver treated sewage water — not drinking water — to construction sites, parks and gardens. The launch happened exactly on schedule, on the utility’s own 37th Foundation Day; government buildings were told to use it, two large private campuses (Mindspace, Raheja) were asked to, and a lake-demolition agency (HYDRAA) was handed the job of checking compliance. What is still missing — a published tariff, a confirmed volume target, and clarity on whether private builders are legally bound or merely invited — is exactly what was missing when this paper first covered the announcement in October, which tells you more about how this government sequences a rollout than any single press release does. El Nino rainfall deficit | v Singur / Manjira reservoirs under stress ---> Govt wants bulk non-drinking users OFF reservoir water | | v v HMWSSB registers private STPs as HMWSSB meets CREDAI/NAREDCO/Builders Fed. certified suppliers (24 Sep) --> announces 1 Nov launch, terms TBD (16 Oct) | | +------------------------ converge ---------------+ | v 1 Nov: Green Water Tanker fleet flagged off (HMWSSB's 37th Foundation Day) | +---------------------+----------------------+ v v Govt premises: MANDATORY use ordered Private campuses: ASKED (Mindspace, Raheja) | | v v HYDRAA deployed to inspect construction-site compliance | v STILL OPEN: tariff, final volume target, legal status for smaller builders | v >>> For Vivek: budget risk until tariff is published; ask HMWSSB's zonal office directly rather than waiting for a notification 1. An announced launch date tells you almost nothing about whether the commercial terms (price, volume, enforcement) are ready — track those separately, and budget against published numbers only, never announcements. 2. When a government wants quiet, durable compliance from an industry, it often starts by naming a handful of large, reputation-sensitive players (Mindspace, Raheja) rather than issuing a blanket order — watch who gets named first as the leading indicator of who faces a mandatory rule next. 3. Enforcement agencies in Telangana are reused across purposes — HYDRAA moving from lake demolitions to water-use inspection is a pattern, not an exception; once an agency exists, expect its remit to grow. 4. A resource crisis (drought) often gets solved by turning a waste product (sewage) into a new regulated market, rather than by pure rationing — whenever you see a scarcity story, ask whether a reuse market is being built alongside the restriction, because that is usually where the business opportunity sits. 5. The same institution can be reliably fast at ceremony (hitting a launch date, flagging off tankers on its own Foundation Day) and reliably slow at substance (tariff, enforcement) — judge a scheme's real maturity by its least glamorous missing piece, not its press event. 2026-11-03|ls-scams: Common land scams in India and how to protect yourself Land School · source: “Common Land Scams in India and How to Protect Yourself” by 1acre.in Key Highlights Fraud thrives where records are scattered: ~95% of RoRs are computerised, but only ~68% of cadastral maps. The deadliest scam is the LEGAL-LOOKING one: registered deeds on assigned land are void — registration proves nothing. Seven patterns cover most of the market: forged titles, restricted land, duplicate sales, PoA abuse, encroachment, benami, fake pre-launch schemes. The defence is always the same: pull the records YOURSELF — RoR, EC, prohibited list, title chain. Remote buyers and absentee owners are the favourite targets. Why India’s land market attracts so much fraud Fraud grows wherever information is scarce and checking is hard. India’s records are digitising UNEVENLY — about 95% of Records of Rights computerised but only 68% of cadastral maps, with some districts still on ageing paper — and every state runs its own system. The favourite victims: buyers unfamiliar with local revenue records, people purchasing remotely, and plots whose owners are absent or unaware something is being sold in their name. The most devastating one: restricted land sold as normal Certain land legally CANNOT be freely sold: government-assigned land, tribal land, ceiling-surplus land, endowment (temple) land, forest land. The scam: a legitimate-looking registered document, payment made, registration completed — and years or decades later the government reclaims the land because it was assigned all along. Buyer loses land, money and everything built on it. The legal trap: the prohibited-list mechanism (Section 22-A) only BLOCKS registration of parcels actually on the Collector’s list — unlisted assigned parcels register fine — but the transfer-ban law voids the sale regardless of what any registrar accepted. So: check the prohibited register AND the revenue record’s remarks, always. Seven scams to know 1) Title fraud and forged documents — the most widespread: a fraudster forges papers, poses as owner or PoA holder, sells land that is not theirs; forged paper carries zero legal weight, which is why the CHAIN matters more than the current deed. 2) Restricted-land sales — as above. 3) Duplicate sales — one plot sold to two or more buyers, exploiting slow registration; not a pure first-to-register race (a deed relates back to its execution date under Section 47), but the genuinely prior sale usually prevails and everyone else litigates. 4) PoA abuse — forged, expired or revoked PoAs used to sell without the owner’s knowledge; an unregistered PoA, or one not clearly authorising sale, is a warning. 5) Encroachment folded in — the boundary shown quietly includes government or neighbouring land; good title to part, nothing on the rest; a boundary survey catches it. 6) Benami deals — property in someone else’s name to hide the real buyer; illegal under the 2016 Benami law, with confiscation and up to seven years’ rigorous imprisonment. 7) Fake pre-launch schemes — units sold in unapproved projects with assured-return promises backed by post-dated cheques that bounce; RERA bars selling before registration, so a pre-launch pitch WITHOUT a RERA number is the tell. Definition — Benami transaction: a purchase held in a name-lender’s name while someone else pays and controls it. Since the 2016 amendment the property can be confiscated outright — buyer-side participation is itself the crime. Red flags and what they mean Warning sign What it usually means What to do Price well below market Defect the seller knows and you don’t Slow down; the discount IS the disclosure Pressure to close fast Verification window being shortened deliberately Never pay before checks complete Seller supplies all documents, resists your own EC pull Papers may be curated or forged Pull EC and RoR yourself from official sources Sale via PoA, owner unreachable Possible PoA abuse or a dead/unaware principal Meet or video-verify the owner; check PoA registration “Registration will fix everything” Confusing registration with valid title Remember: void transfers register too No RERA number on a project pitch Unapproved / pre-launch scheme Verify on the state RERA portal before any token Documents to check before any purchase ☐ Title + sale deed — seller’s name matches the record; chain traced 30 years. ☐ Record of Rights — owner, classification, mutation history, restriction remarks. ☐ EC — pulled by YOU from the sub-registrar; never the seller’s copy. ☐ Land use / conversion — classification confirmed; conversion completed if it was agricultural. ☐ Mutation — updated, no restriction notes. ☐ Tax receipts — dues attach to the LAND, not the old owner. ☐ RERA — verified on the portal for any plotted or builder project. ☐ PoA, if involved — authorises sale, registered where required, traceable to the real owner. What maps can and cannot catch Survey-number maps, master-plan overlays and satellite imagery catch boundary and zoning mismatches — whether the parcel’s ground reality matches the deed, and whether it sits in a restricted zone — before a site visit. They cannot read a title chain, tell a forged deed from a genuine one, or check the prohibited list. That work stays with the sub-registrar’s records and a revenue-law advocate. Quick answers (FAQ) Most common scam? Title fraud with forged documents. How do I know if land has transfer restrictions? RoR remarks + the state’s prohibited-property register. Can I buy through a PoA? Yes, with independent verification of the PoA and the principal — PoA sales are not inherently illegitimate. What if I unknowingly bought restricted land? The transfer is void; get a revenue advocate immediately. Is RERA-registered land always safe? Safer — but RERA checks the project, not the title chain; do both. How to report fraud? Police complaint (EOW for large frauds) + civil suit; registration of a case does not undo the transfer, so prevention is the real remedy. Bottom line Nearly every land scam succeeds at the same moment: when the buyer accepts someone else’s paperwork instead of pulling their own. RoR, EC, prohibited list, 30-year chain, boundary survey — five self-service checks defeat all seven scams. For you: Your buyers fear exactly this list — which makes it your marketing. A venture that publishes its own verification file (chain, EC, prohibited-list clearance, DTCP approval) sells trust the unorganised market cannot. Internally: rule — no landowner conversation advances until the RoR and prohibited-list check are done, however warm the introduction. 2026-11-03|ls-dtcp: DTCP approval explained: what it means for plot buyers Land School · source: “DTCP Approval Explained: What It Means for Plot Buyers” by 1acre.in Key Highlights DTCP approval is a LAYOUT permit under state town-planning law — it certifies road width, open-space reservation, zoning and infrastructure. It does NOT certify title. WHICH authority approves depends on where the plot sits — metropolitan areas have their own authorities; DTCP covers the rest. The verification is the LP NUMBER, searched by you on the official portal. A brochure claim is not evidence. A FILE number is not an LP number — “approval in process” means unapproved today. Roads and OSR land inside an approved layout belong to the local body and cannot be sold as plots. What DTCP approval actually certifies A layout permit issued by the Directorate of Town and Country Planning under the state’s town-planning law, confirming the layout meets planning and development standards: road widths, zoning compliance, open spaces, infrastructure provisions. What it never touches: who OWNS the land. An approved layout on a disputed title is still a disputed title with nice roads. Definition — OSR (Open Space Reservation): the share of a layout — typically around 10% — that must be set aside for parks and public purposes and vested in the local body. It is the community’s land; a developer selling “plots” carved from it is selling what is not theirs. DTCP does not apply everywhere The commonest error is checking the right number against the WRONG authority. DTCP’s writ covers the state MINUS the metropolitan planning areas — in Chennai that belt belongs to CMDA; in Hyderabad, HMDA approves inside its boundary while DTCP covers the districts beyond, alongside local and new-town planning authorities issuing equally valid approvals under the same law. First question for any plot: WHOSE jurisdiction is this survey number in? How to verify using the LP number Ask the seller for the approval PROCEEDINGS ORDER and the LP number with its year. Then search it YOURSELF: Telangana — dtcp.telangana.gov.in or the DPMS district-wise approved-layout lists (HMDA’s portal for its belt); Tamil Nadu — onlineppa.tn.gov.in or tcp.tn.gov.in. Older records (roughly ten years plus) often move from the regional office to central storage — an RTI or counter application becomes the route. Then MATCH: survey numbers on the portal against the sale deed; road widths, plot numbers and OSR positions on the approved plan against what is being shown on-site. The plan on the portal is the contract; the site should be its photocopy. Which authority approves what Where the plot sits Approving authority Where to search Metropolitan planning area (e.g. HMDA belt / CMDA) The metropolitan authority Its own approved-layout portal Rest of the state DTCP State DTCP portal / DPMS lists Notified local planning areas Local / new-town planning authority That authority’s records Gram panchayat areas Still the competent planning authority Panchayat “sanction” alone is NOT layout approval The traps that cost buyers money “Approval is in process” — the layout is unapproved TODAY; the number offered is usually a file/application number, and a file number returns nothing on the portal. Gram-panchayat sanction dressed as approval — a panchayat has no power to approve a layout; this is the single most documented fraud pattern in plot sales. OSR and road land sold as plots — reserved areas belong to the local body; corner plots adjoining a reserved zone are where the boundary gets blurred. “Regularisation applied for” — applying under regularisation rules does not make a layout approved; wait for the FINAL order. Approved layout on unconverted land — layout approval and agricultural-land conversion are separate; confirm the conversion order separately. Example: A ₹28-lakh “DTCP-approved” plot near Shadnagar: the brochure prints “LP No. — applied” and a gram-panchayat resolution. Portal search: nothing. Two years later the regularisation application is rejected, the layout stays unapproved, banks refuse loans against every plot in it, and resale prices halve. The five-minute portal search was the whole due diligence. Your checklist before you pay ☐ Confirm which planning authority governs the location. ☐ Get the approval proceedings order + LP number with year. ☐ Search the LP number YOURSELF on the portal; keep the printout. ☐ Match survey numbers, road widths, OSR positions against deed and site. ☐ Treat “in process” and “regularisation applied” as UNAPPROVED. ☐ Run title chain, patta and EC checks separately — approval is not ownership. Quick answers (FAQ) Is approval mandatory before buying? For a safe, financeable, resalable plot — effectively yes. Home loan without it? Banks generally refuse plots in unapproved layouts. Does approval mean clear title? No — planning compliance only. If I buy unapproved anyway? Loan rejection, registration obstacles in some states, regularisation charges if a window opens, demolition exposure if it never does — and a permanent discount at resale. Bottom line One number, one portal, five minutes, your own eyes: the LP-number search is the highest-value check in plot buying. Everything a brochure claims is marketing until the portal agrees. For you: This is YOUR licence to operate — your ventures’ LP numbers are the moat that separates you from the unapproved-layout market. Print the LP number and approved plan into every marketing piece and teach buyers to verify it themselves: the developer who INVITES verification wins the trust war at zero cost. 2026-11-05|dd-sadar-sammelanam: DEEP DIVE OF THE DAY Revanth Reddy Sanctions ₹5 Crore For The Yadav Community’s Sadar Sammelanam — Then Uses The Stage To Ask The Same Community To Back Musi Rejuvenation, Metro Phase-2 And Bharat Future City, Telangana’s Three Biggest Live Land Projects 1. The story, explained from zero — fact by fact Direct WebFetch to every outlet carrying this story (ANI, Siasat, Daily Pioneer, Deccan Chronicle) was blocked by this environment’s network proxy today. What follows is built fact-by-fact from cross-checked WebSearch result summaries, restated in plain words — never a verbatim quote from any original article except the Chief Minister’s and Tejashwi Yadav’s own direct statements, which are reproduced because they were themselves reported as direct quotes — with every claim checked against at least one other independent search result before being included. 12 distinct facts were found worth unpacking; all 12 are covered below. S1 · The event and venue On Wednesday, 4 November 2026, Hyderabad’s Yadav community held its annual Sadar Sammelanam — a Deepavali buffalo-carnival — at NTR Gardens, organised by the Sri Krishna Sadar Sammelan Utsav Committee. Plain English: this is a long-running community festival, not a one-off political rally — the politics was layered onto an existing cultural event. Mechanics: a community committee organises the event logistics; government ministers and leaders attend as guests and speakers, which is how a cultural festival becomes a platform for political messaging. S2 · The money and the status The state government sanctioned ₹5 crore for this year’s Sadar Sammelanam celebrations and formally declared the event an official state festival. Plain English: the government didn’t just attend — it paid for the event and gave it a permanent official status, which is a bigger and more durable commitment than a one-time grant. Mechanics: “state festival” status typically means recurring government funding and official calendar recognition in future years, not just this one. Incentives: this is a low-cost, high-visibility way to build goodwill with a specific community ahead of asking that community for something larger. Numbers: ₹5 crore is a small sum next to the tens of thousands of crores involved in Musi Rejuvenation or Bharat Future City — the value here is political, not financial. S3 · The Chief Minister’s framing of the festival Revanth Reddy told the gathering that the Sadar Sammelanam is not merely a festival of the Yadav community, but a celebration of the self-respect of all the people of Telangana. Plain English: he deliberately widened the frame from “one community’s festival” to “everyone’s pride,” a common rhetorical move when a leader wants a community-specific gesture to read as statesmanship rather than narrow vote-bank politics. S4 · Credit for building Hyderabad The Chief Minister credited the Yadav community with having helped Hyderabad develop into the city it is today. Plain English: a broad statement of historical gratitude, with no specific claim, project or data point attached to verify it against. S5 · The Golconda Fort/‘Yadav kings’ claim Revanth Reddy pointed to Golconda Fort as a site from the Yadav era, saying it was Yadav kings who governed the Kakatiya dynasty. Plain English: this is presented as a point of community pride and shared heritage. Mechanics/accuracy check: mainstream historical sourcing (including the Archaeological Survey of India’s own account and standard reference works) attributes Golconda’s original fort to the Kakatiya dynasty itself, later expanded by the Bahmani Sultanate and then the Qutb Shahi dynasty — none of which independent sourcing describes as a “Yadav dynasty.” The Kakatiyas and the historical Yadava (Seuna) dynasty of Devagiri were two separate, contemporaneous ruling houses in Deccan history, not one and the same. Glossary — every term, simply Sadar Sammelanam An annual Deepavali-season buffalo-carnival festival celebrated by Hyderabad’s Yadav community, now also an officially recognised state festival with government funding attached. State festival status An official government declaration that elevates a community or regional celebration to the state’s own calendar of recognised events, typically bringing recurring public funding and formal government participation in future editions, not just a one-time grant. Riverbed and buffer zone The riverbed is the land the river physically occupies, including when it is dry; the buffer zone is a protective margin of land around it kept clear for flood safety and ecological reasons. Structures built inside either are, by definition, built somewhere construction was never meant to be legally permanent. Rehabilitation and Resettlement (R&R) The process of relocating people displaced by a government project to alternative housing or land, usually alongside some form of compensation — distinct from simply evicting them with no replacement arrangement. Social Impact Assessment (SIA) A mandatory study, normally required under India’s central land acquisition law, of exactly who will be displaced by a project and how, which must usually be completed before large government land acquisition proceeds — unless the project is specifically exempted from it by government order, as parts of the Musi project reportedly have been. Patta land Land for which the holder has an official government-issued ownership record (a patta) — the baseline paper proof of lawful private title that farmers resisting Future City acquisition say covers roughly 2,200 acres of the contested area. High Court stay order A court direction pausing a specific government action — here, land acquisition or possession — while a case challenging it is still being heard; it is not a final ruling on who is right, only a freeze until the court decides. Caste-based political outreach (‘vote-bank’ politics) The practice of directing government recognition, funding or promises specifically toward a caste or community group in exchange for its political support — a long-standing and widely practised feature of Indian electoral politics, visible here in the funding and representation promises made to the Yadav community. RJD (Rashtriya Janata Dal) A Bihar-based regional political party, led by the Yadav family, that has historically drawn much of its support from Bihar’s Yadav and Muslim communities. Special Area Development Authority A planning body a state government can set up for a defined geographic area outside existing municipal or metropolitan-development-authority jurisdictions, with its own powers over layouts, approvals and land allotments — the kind of authority structure used to administer large new-city projects like Bharat Future City. 4. 2026-11-05|ls-boundary: How to resolve land boundary disputes using survey records Land School · source: “How to Resolve Land Boundary Disputes Using Survey Records” by 1acre.in Key Highlights Most boundary fights trace to outdated surveys, vague old deeds, or inherited land split informally without fresh measurement. Cadastral maps and Field Measurement Books carry more weight in these disputes than any other evidence. A fresh official survey from the revenue department is the FIRST move, not the last resort. Twelve years of open hostile possession can ripen into adverse possession — delay has a price in land, not just time. Digitisation is real but uneven: ~95% of RoRs computerised, ~68% of maps, geo-referencing at ~49%. Why these disputes keep happening Outdated or inconsistent records; ambiguous boundary descriptions in older sale deeds; inherited property subdivided informally without fresh surveys; delayed mutation. Many records originate in the colonial era, and though the national modernisation drive (DILRMP) has digitised much, progress is uneven — leaving some areas running on decades-old measurements while land prices around them multiplied. Survey records: where every resolution starts Two records outrank everything else. The cadastral map — the official parcel map identifying each survey number and its neighbours. The Field Measurement Book (FMB) — the recorded measurements from official surveys of each parcel. Together with title documents and revenue records, these are what authorities and courts use to determine where one property legally ends and the next begins — and they beat personal recollections and “the old tamarind tree” descriptions every time. Definition — Field Measurement Book (FMB): the survey department’s measurement sketch of a single survey number — sides, angles, extent. In a boundary fight it is the closest thing to ground truth on paper. Probate stopped being MANDATORY anywhere in India on 20 December 2025 (Repealing and Amending Act, 2025 removed Section 213) — but banks and buyers still ask for it. India has no transfer-on-death deed; the nearest equivalent is a registered settlement or gift deed made while the owner is alive. Why ownership does not transfer automatically An heir does not become the recorded owner by grief alone — someone has to FILE, and the filing is mutation: updating the revenue and municipal record so the state knows who now owes land revenue and property tax. The application goes to the concerned revenue authority with the death certificate, proof of heirship, and the existing land records. With a will vs without one With a will: land passes directly to named beneficiaries through the executor — sometimes involving probate. Without a will (intestate): ownership follows the personal succession law of the deceased’s religion — the Hindu Succession Act for Hindus (daughters holding EQUAL coparcenary rights since 2005), Muslim personal law with its fixed shares, the Indian Succession Act for Christians and Parsis. The intestate route usually needs court-issued heirship paperwork, making it slower — which is the practical argument for a will. Definition — Probate: a court’s certification that a will is genuine. Since 20 December 2025 it is mandatory NOWHERE in India — the old Section 213 requirement (which bound certain wills, notably in the presidency towns) was repealed. But the market has memory: banks and cautious buyers still ASK for probate on willed property, so sometimes heirs obtain it for smoothness even though the law no longer compels it. Legal-heir certificate vs succession certificate Constantly confused, differently scoped. A legal-heir certificate establishes WHO the heirs are — used for utility transfers, pensions, bank formalities, and as the heirship proof in land mutation. A succession certificate , issued by a civil court, authorises the holder to collect the deceased’s DEBTS, SECURITIES and MOVABLE assets — it does not itself convey land. Why India has no transfer-on-death deed — and the substitute Several countries let owners name a death-beneficiary on the deed itself; India does not. The working equivalent: a registered settlement or gift deed executed while the owner is alive , reserving a LIFE INTEREST — the owner keeps possession until death, and the property vests in the named person automatically afterwards. A sister objects, the revenue officer freezes the entry, and the file crosses into civil-court territory — two years gone. The written NOCs would have cost a week. Selling inherited land Most inherited land eventually reaches the market — and that is where unfinished mutation surfaces, because any buyer’s verification matches seller against record, and the record still names the deceased. Heirs who complete mutation BEFORE listing sell on their own timeline; those who do not discover the gap at the sub-registrar, in front of their buyer. Not in India — use a registered settlement/gift deed with life interest. Do daughters have equal rights? Yes — equal coparcenary rights in Hindu law since 2005. How long does it take? Certificate, heirship, NOCs, EC, mutation — done early, in order, it is administration; done late or out of order, it is litigation. If not, your timeline is not theirs to promise. And structurally: an incomplete heir set signing your agreement is a future injunction on your layout — collect every heir’s signature or a court partition first.
